claim: Protein kinases are major drug targets.
source: Protein kinases are major drug targets, but the development of highly-selective inhibitors has been challenging due to the similarity of their active sites.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and is supported by citations in the introduction (Cohen, 2002; Hopkins and Groom, 2002).

claim: The development of highly-selective kinase inhibitors has been challenging due to the similarity of their active sites.
source: Protein kinases are major drug targets, but the development of highly-selective inhibitors has been challenging due to the similarity of their active sites.
evidence: This is a well-established challenge in the field, stated in the abstract.

claim: The DFG loop can adopt distinct structural states.
source: The observation of distinct structural states of the fully-conserved Asp-Phe-Gly (DFG) loop has put the concept of conformational selection for the DFG-state at the center of kinase drug discovery.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and supported by crystallographic data presented in the manuscript.

claim: Gleevec selectivity for Abl was rooted in conformational changes after drug binding rather than conformational selection.
source: Recently, it was shown that Gleevec selectivity for the Tyr-kinase Abl was instead rooted in conformational changes after drug binding.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract and references prior work (Agafonov et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2015).

claim: Protein dynamics in the drug-bound state plays a crucial role in drug selectivity, affinity, and on-target residence time for kinase inhibitors.
source: These new concepts, where protein dynamics in the drug-bound state plays the crucial role, can be applied to inhibitor design of targets outside the kinome.
evidence: This is the main conclusion stated in the abstract and supported by the kinetic data presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Protein kinases have become the number one drug target of the 21st century.
source: Protein kinases have become the number one drug target of the 21th century (Cohen, 2002; Hopkins and Groom, 2002), due to their central role in cellular processes and involvement in various types of cancer (Carvajal et al., 2006; Gautschi et al., 2008; Katayama and Sen, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Protein kinases play a central role in cellular processes and are involved in various types of cancer.
source: Protein kinases have become the number one drug target of the 21th century (Cohen, 2002; Hopkins and Groom, 2002), due to their central role in cellular processes and involvement in various types of cancer (Carvajal et al., 2006; Gautschi et al., 2008; Katayama and Sen, 2010).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Gleevec is a highly selective drug that specifically targets Abl kinase.
source: One of the biggest success stories is Gleevec: a highly selective drug that specifically targets Abl kinase, providing an efficient treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and minimizing side effects (Iqbal and Iqbal, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Gleevec provides an efficient treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and minimizes side effects.
source: One of the biggest success stories is Gleevec: a highly selective drug that specifically targets Abl kinase, providing an efficient treatment of chronic myelogenous leukemia (CML) and minimizing side effects (Iqbal and Iqbal, 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Gleevec can only bind to an inactive DFG loop conformation in the 'out-conformation' due to steric clash of the active, DFG-in conformation.
source: Seminal work by the Kuriyan lab demonstrated that Gleevec can only bind to an inactive DFG (for Asp-Phe-Gly) loop conformation in the 'out-conformation' due to steric clash of the active, DFG-in conformation (Nagar et al., 2002; Schindler et al., 2000; Seeliger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The conformational state of the DFG loop has been proposed to dictate the selectivity for Gleevec and other kinase inhibitors.
source: Since then it has long been proposed that the conformational state of the fully-conserved DFG loop (Taylor et al., 2012) dictates the selectivity for Gleevec and other kinase inhibitors (Lovera et al., 2012; Nagar et al., 2002; Schindler et al., 2000; Treiber and Shah, 2013; Xu et al., 1997).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The orientation of the DFG-motif and its possible steric clashes proved insufficient to explain drug selectivity and affinity.
source: The orientation of the DFG-motif and its possible steric clashes is indeed important for the ability of a class of inhibitors to bind to the kinase, but proved insufficient to explain drug selectivity and affinity.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a conclusion from prior work.

claim: An induced-fit step after drug binding is the key determinant for Gleevec's selectivity.
source: Recent quantitative binding kinetics combined with ancestral sequence reconstruction put forward a mechanism where an induced-fit step after drug binding is the key determinant for Gleevec's selectivity (Agafonov et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2015), and fully recapitulates the binding affinities.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Aurora A kinase is a key regulator of mitotic events, including mitotic entry, centrosome maturation and spindle formation.
source: Aurora A kinase is one of the key regulators of mitotic events, including mitotic entry, centrosome maturation and spindle formation (Fu et al., 2007; Lukasiewicz and Lingle, 2009; Marumoto et al., 2005), as well as assisting in neuronal migration (Nikonova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Aurora A assists in neuronal migration.
source: Aurora A kinase is one of the key regulators of mitotic events, including mitotic entry, centrosome maturation and spindle formation (Fu et al., 2007; Lukasiewicz and Lingle, 2009; Marumoto et al., 2005), as well as assisting in neuronal migration (Nikonova et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Aurora A is overexpressed in a wide range of tumors, including breast, colon, ovary and skin malignancies.
source: Aurora A has attracted significant attention for the development of targeted agents for cancer because it is overexpressed in a wide range of tumors, including breast, colon, ovary and skin malignancies (Carvajal et al., 2006; Gautschi et al., 2008; Katayama and Sen, 2010; Lok et al., 2010; Marzo and Naval, 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Danusertib (PHA739358) inhibits all members of the Aurora family with low nanomolar IC50 values (13, 79 and 61 nM for Aurora A, B and C, respectively).
source: Danusertib (PHA739358) and AT9283 were developed for Aurora kinases, whereas Gleevec is selective for the Tyr kinase Abl. Danusertib inhibits all members of the Aurora family with low nanomolar IC50 values (13, 79 and 61 nM for Aurora A, B and C, respectively) (Carpinelli et al., 2007; Fraedrich et al., 2012) and was one of the first Aurora kinase inhibitors to enter phase I and II clinical trials (Kollareddy et al., 2012; Steeghs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: Danusertib was one of the first Aurora kinase inhibitors to enter phase I and II clinical trials.
source: Danusertib inhibits all members of the Aurora family with low nanomolar IC50 values (13, 79 and 61 nM for Aurora A, B and C, respectively) (Carpinelli et al., 2007; Fraedrich et al., 2012) and was one of the first Aurora kinase inhibitors to enter phase I and II clinical trials (Kollareddy et al., 2012; Steeghs et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A crystal structure of Danusertib bound to Aurora A kinase shows an inactive kinase with the DFG-loop in the out conformation.
source: A crystal structure of Danusertib bound to Aurora A kinase shows an inactive kinase with the DFG-loop in the out conformation (Fancelli et al., 2006).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: AT9283 inhibits both Aurora A and B with an IC50 of 3 nM.
source: AT9283 inhibits both Aurora A and B with an IC50 of 3 nM (Howard et al., 2009) and has also entered several clinical trials (Borisa and Bhatt, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: AT9283 has entered several clinical trials.
source: AT9283 inhibits both Aurora A and B with an IC50 of 3 nM (Howard et al., 2009) and has also entered several clinical trials (Borisa and Bhatt, 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: The crystal structure of Aurora A with AT9283 shows that this drug binds to the DFG-in, active conformation of the kinase.
source: Interestingly, the crystal structure of Aurora A with AT9283 shows that this drug binds to the DFG-in, active conformation of the kinase (Howard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Two crystals from the same crystallization well capture both the inactive and active conformations of dephosphorylated Aurora A bound with AMPPCP.
source: Two crystals from the same crystallization well capture both the inactive and active conformations of dephosphorylated Aurora A bound with AMPPCP (Figure 1A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1A,B showing the two structures.

claim: The first structure (PDB 4C3R) superimposes with the well-known inactive, dephosphorylated Aurora A structure (PDB 1MUO).
source: As anticipated, the first structure (PDB 4C3R [Zorba et al., 2014]) superimposes with the well-known inactive, dephosphorylated Aurora A structure (PDB 1MUO [Cheetham et al., 2002]) and the activation loop is not visible as commonly observed for kinases lacking phosphorylation of the activation loop (Zorba et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The second structure (PDB 6CPF) adopts the same conformation as the previously published phosphorylated, active structure (PDB 1OL7).
source: The second structure (PDB 6CPF; Table 1) adopts the same conformation as the previously published phosphorylated, active structure (PDB 1OL7 [Bayliss et al., 2003]) (Figure 1C) and the first part of the activation loop could be built, although the B-factors are high.
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation and reference to Figure 1C.

claim: Every hallmark of an active state is seen for dephosphorylated Aurora A, including the DFG-in conformation that is essential for completing the regulatory spine.
source: Every hallmark of an active state is seen for this dephosphorylated protein, including the DFG-in conformation that is essential for completing the regulatory spine.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the crystal structure data.

claim: In the active, non-phosphorylated structure, electron density is seen in the canonical tighter Mg2+-binding site, where the metal ion is coordinated to the α- and β-phosphates of AMPPCP and Asp274.
source: In the active, non-phosphorylated structure, electron density is seen in the canonical tighter Mg2+-binding site, where the metal ion is coordinated to the α- and β-phosphates of AMPPCP and Asp274.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on crystallographic data.

claim: In the inactive structure, no electron density for Mg2+ can be identified possibly due to the fact that Asp274 is rotated to the DFG-out position.
source: In the inactive structure, no electron density for Mg2+ can be identified possibly due to the fact that Asp274 is rotated to the DFG-out position and is, therefore, lost as coordination partner.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on crystallographic data and structural reasoning.

claim: Sampling of the active conformation does not depend on AMPPCP binding as dephosphorylated, apo Aurora A also crystallizes in the active form.
source: Furthermore, sampling of the active conformation does not depend on AMPPCP binding as dephosphorylated, apo Aurora A also crystallizes in the active form (PDB 6CPE; Figure 1E,F and Table 1).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by the crystal structure (PDB 6CPE) and Figure 1E,F.

claim: Wild-type, dephosphorylated Aurora A in its apo or nucleotide bound state has been found in the active conformation in other crystallographic studies.
source: Our results are consistent with other crystallographic studies on wild-type, dephosphorylated Aurora A in its apo or nucleotide bound state, where the kinase was also found in the active conformation (Gustafson et al., 2014; Janeček et al., 2016; Nowakowski et al., 2002).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: In Aurora kinase sequences a tryptophan residue, Trp277, is immediately following the DFG motif and displays a drastically different orientation whether Aurora A is in an active (DFG-in) or inactive (DFG-out) conformation.
source: We note that in Aurora kinase sequences a tryptophan residue, Trp277, is immediately following the DFG motif and displays a drastically different orientation whether Aurora A is in an active (DFG-in) or inactive (DFG-out) conformation (Figure 1D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 1D showing the structural differences.

claim: Trp277 is unique for the Aurora kinase family in the Ser/Thr kinome.
source: This Trp moiety is unique for the Aurora kinase family in the Ser/Thr kinome and its position is suggested to be important for tuning the substrate specificity (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The position of Trp277 is suggested to be important for tuning the substrate specificity.
source: This Trp moiety is unique for the Aurora kinase family in the Ser/Thr kinome and its position is suggested to be important for tuning the substrate specificity (Chen et al., 2014).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Only three out of four tryptophan side chain indole signals are seen in the 2D NMR spectra of a [15N]-Trp labeled sample of Aurora A.
source: [1H-15N]-TROSY-HSQC experiments on uniformly 15N-labeled samples of Aurora A proved to be no exception: many peaks are missing and only three out of four tryptophan side chain indole signals are seen in the 2D spectra of a [15N]-Trp labeled sample (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2A,B showing the NMR spectra.

claim: Four peaks are observed in 19F NMR spectra for apo- and AMPPCP-bound wild-type Aurora A containing 5-fluoro-tryptophan residues.
source: Aurora A was produced containing 5-fluoro-tryptophan residues to allow for one-dimensional 19F spectroscopy to deal with exchange broadening while providing sensitivity close to proton NMR (Kitevski-LeBlanc and Prosser, 2012). Now, we observe as expected four peaks in our NMR spectra for apo- and AMPPCP-bound wild-type Aurora A (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2C showing the 19F NMR spectra.

claim: The linewidth of one resonance in the 19F NMR spectrum is approximately 5-fold larger than the others.
source: A deconvolution of the spectrum yields almost identical integral values for all four peaks, whereas the linewidth of one resonance is approximately 5-fold larger (Figure 2D, purple signal).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 2D showing the deconvolution.

claim: The broad peak in the 19F NMR spectrum originates from Trp277, directly adjacent to the DFG-loop.
source: This broad peak is a prime candidate to originate from Trp277, directly adjacent to the DFG-loop. The W277L mutation confirmed our hypothesis (Figure 2C), and the extensive line broadening of this signal in a one-dimensional spectrum is consistent with its absence in the [1H,15N]-TROSY-HSQC spectrum.
evidence: This is stated in the results section and confirmed by mutagenesis data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: The W277L mutant is still active, as confirmed by a kinase assay.
source: Of note, the W277L mutant is still active, as confirmed by a kinase assay, most likely because this Trp is not conserved in Ser/Thr kinases, where a Leu residue is found at that position for several Ser/Thr family members.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on kinase assay data.

claim: The broad line shape for the Trp277 peak hints at severe exchange broadening in the surrounding of the DFG-loop.
source: The broad line shape for the Trp277 peak hints at severe exchange broadening in the surrounding of the DFG-loop and is consistent with the high B-factors for Trp277 and its neighboring residues observed in all crystal structures described here.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on NMR and crystallographic data.

claim: Binding kinetics of Gleevec to Aurora A exhibited biphasic kinetic traces at 10°C.
source: At 25°C, the binding of Gleevec to Aurora A was too fast to be monitored and, therefore, experiments were performed at 10°C. Binding kinetics of Gleevec to Aurora A exhibited biphasic kinetic traces (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 3A showing the kinetic traces.

claim: The second, slow phase of Gleevec binding exhibits an increase in fluorescence intensity.
source: The second, slow phase exhibits an increase in fluorescence intensity (Figure 3A), with the observed rate constant decreasing with Gleevec concentration (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figures 3A and 3D.

claim: These rate constants represent the conformational change from DFG-in to -out and vice versa since Gleevec is a DFG-out selective inhibitor due to steric hindrance.
source: These rate constants represent the conformational change from DFG-in to -out and vice versa since Gleevec is a DFG-out selective inhibitor due to steric hindrance (Nagar et al., 2002; Schindler et al., 2000; Seeliger et al., 2007).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with supporting citations.

claim: The lack of an induced-fit step for Gleevec binding to Aurora A is the major reason for Gleevec's weak binding.
source: In summary, the lack of an induced-fit step for Gleevec binding to Aurora A is the major reason for Gleevec's weak binding, and not the DFG-loop conformation or physical drug-binding step, consistent with our earlier results (Wilson et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the kinetic data.

claim: An increase in fluorescence intensity was observed at all Danusertib concentrations and showed double-exponential behavior.
source: An increase in fluorescence intensity was observed at all Danusertib concentrations and showed double-exponential behavior (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5B showing the kinetic traces.

claim: The dependence of one of the observed rate constants on Danusertib concentration is linear.
source: The dependence of the two observed rates constants on drug concentration is linear for one of them (Figure 5C) and non-linear for the other with an apparent plateau at approximately 16 ± 2 s−1 (Figure 5D).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5C showing the linear dependence.

claim: The step with linear inhibitor concentration dependence corresponds to the second-order binding step.
source: The step with linear inhibitor concentration dependence corresponds to the second-order binding step, whereas a non-linear concentration dependency hints at protein conformational transitions.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on kinetic analysis.

claim: The slow-off rate of Danusertib from Aurora A is k-3 = (3.2 ± 0.3) × 10−4 s−1.
source: Next, the dissociation kinetics for Danusertib was measured by fluorescence and appeared to be extremely slow with an observed slow-off rate of (3.2 ± 0.3) × 10−4 s−1 (Figure 5E).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 5E showing the dissociation kinetics.

claim: A conformational selection mechanism always weakens the overall inhibitor affinity.
source: Our results illuminate trivial but profound principles of binding affinity and lifetime of drug/target complexes: a conformational selection mechanism always weakens the overall inhibitor affinity, while an induced-fit step tightens the affinity depending on how far-shifted the equilibrium in the enzyme/drug complex is (Equations 2–4, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2 showing the effect on KD.

claim: An induced-fit step tightens the affinity depending on how far-shifted the equilibrium in the enzyme/drug complex is.
source: Our results illuminate trivial but profound principles of binding affinity and lifetime of drug/target complexes: a conformational selection mechanism always weakens the overall inhibitor affinity, while an induced-fit step tightens the affinity depending on how far-shifted the equilibrium in the enzyme/drug complex is (Equations 2–4, Figure 6—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 6—figure supplement 2.

claim: For DFG-out binders, the DFG-in and -out equilibrium weakens the overall affinity 1.6-fold.
source: For DFG-out binders (e.g., Danusertib and Gleevec), the DFG-in and -out equilibrium weakens the overall affinity 1.6-fold; however, the conformational change after drug binding results in a four orders of magnitude tighter binding for Danusertib and is the sole reason for its high affinity to Aurora A compared to Gleevec.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the kinetic data.

claim: The conformational change after drug binding results in a four orders of magnitude tighter binding for Danusertib and is the sole reason for its high affinity to Aurora A compared to Gleevec.
source: For DFG-out binders (e.g., Danusertib and Gleevec), the DFG-in and -out equilibrium weakens the overall affinity 1.6-fold; however, the conformational change after drug binding results in a four orders of magnitude tighter binding for Danusertib and is the sole reason for its high affinity to Aurora A compared to Gleevec.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the kinetic data.

claim: Rapid kinetic experiments of binding AT9283 to Aurora A at 25°C resulted in biphasic traces and both processes showed an increase in fluorescence over time.
source: Rapid kinetic experiments of binding AT9283 to Aurora A at 25°C resulted in biphasic traces and both processes showed an increase in fluorescence over time (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7A showing the kinetic traces.

claim: Dissociation of AT9283 from Aurora A is characterized by double-exponential kinetics.
source: Dissociation is characterized by double-exponential kinetics (Figure 7D and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7D showing the dissociation kinetics.

claim: The fast phase of AT9283 dissociation decays with a rate constant of (1.1 ± 0.02) × 10−2 s−1.
source: The fast phase (~38% of the total amplitude change) decays with a rate constant of (1.1 ± 0.02) × 10−2 s−1, and the slow phase (~62% of the total change in amplitude) has a rate constant of (0.1 ± 0.01) × 10−2 s−1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the dissociation kinetics data.

claim: The slow phase of AT9283 dissociation has a rate constant of (0.1 ± 0.01) × 10−2 s−1.
source: The fast phase (~38% of the total amplitude change) decays with a rate constant of (1.1 ± 0.02) × 10−2 s−1, and the slow phase (~62% of the total change in amplitude) has a rate constant of (0.1 ± 0.01) × 10−2 s−1.
evidence: This is stated in the results section based on the dissociation kinetics data.

claim: AT9283 can bind to both DFG-in and DFG-out states of Aurora A, but only AurAin:AT can undergo an induced-fit step.
source: These failures, together with the lack of a detectable conformational selection step, led to a new model in which both the DFG-in and DFG-out states can bind AT9283, but only AurAin:AT can undergo an induced-fit step (Figure 7H).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 7H showing the binding scheme.

claim: A crystal structure of AT9283 bound to Aurora A shows the DFG-out conformation.
source: In an effort to structurally verify our model we solved a crystal structure of Aurora A with AT9283 bound and indeed observed the DFG-out conformation (PDB 6CPG, Figure 9B and Table 1), in contrast to the DFG-in conformation as previously reported (Figure 9A) (Howard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 9B showing the crystal structure.

claim: The new crystal structure of AT9283 bound to Aurora A is in contrast to the DFG-in conformation as previously reported.
source: In an effort to structurally verify our model we solved a crystal structure of Aurora A with AT9283 bound and indeed observed the DFG-out conformation (PDB 6CPG, Figure 9B and Table 1), in contrast to the DFG-in conformation as previously reported (Figure 9A) (Howard et al., 2009).
evidence: This is stated in the results section with a supporting citation and Figures 9A and 9B.

claim: The structural and kinetic data together support that AT9283 can bind to both DFG-in and DFG-out state of Aurora A.
source: Thus, our structural and kinetic data together support that AT9283 can bind to both DFG-in and DFG-out state of Aurora A, and emphasizes the need for caution when interpreting single X-ray structures.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the structural and kinetic data.

claim: The binding of mant-ATP to Aurora A showed biphasic kinetic traces.
source: The binding of mant-ATP to Aurora A showed biphasic kinetic traces (Figure 10A) that describe the physical binding step (i.e., linear dependence on mant-ATP concentration; Figure 10B) and the induced-fit step (Figure 10C).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by Figure 10A showing the kinetic traces.

claim: Mant-ATP can bind to both the DFG-in and -out conformations.
source: We find that mant-ATP can bind to both the DFG-in and -out conformations, consistent with our nucleotide-bound crystal structures (Figure 1A–D) and recent single-molecule fluorescence spectroscopy data that indicates that nucleotide binding does not significantly affect this equilibrium (Cyphers et al., 2017).
evidence: This is stated in the results section and supported by crystal structures and a citation.

claim: The presence of an induced-fit step for the natural substrate ATP suggests that such conformational change after ligand binding is a built-in property of the enzyme.
source: The presence of an induced-fit step for the natural substrate ATP suggests that such conformational change after ligand binding is a built-in property of the enzyme.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the ATP binding data.

claim: Inhibitors take advantage of the inherent plasticity of the enzyme that is required for its activity and regulation.
source: In other words, inhibitors take advantage of the inherent plasticity of the enzyme that is required for its activity and regulation.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as an inference from the comparison of ATP and inhibitor binding.

claim: Slow conformational changes, particularly the reverse induced-fit step, are at the heart of action for an efficient drug, because it results in tight binding and a long lifetime on the target.
source: Faster conformational changes and weaker binding are of course prerequisites for efficient turnover; whereas slow conformational changes, particularly the reverse induced-fit step, are at the heart of action for an efficient drug, because it results in tight binding and a long lifetime on the target.
evidence: This is stated in the results section as a conclusion from the kinetic data.

claim: An induced-fit step turns out to be key for all tight-binding inhibitors studied.
source: An induced-fit step turns out to be key for all tight-binding inhibitors studied.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a conclusion from the study.

claim: The induced-fit mechanism may be a general mechanism for different kinases and multiple inhibitors.
source: From our results on Aurora A kinase presented here and earlier data on Tyrosine-kinases (Agafonov et al., 2014; Wilson et al., 2015), we propose that this may be a general mechanism for different kinases and multiple inhibitors, thereby providing a platform for future computational and experimental efforts in rational drug design.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a proposal based on the current and prior data.

claim: A highly-skewed equilibrium towards E*:D increases the affinity for the drug by this coupled equilibrium.
source: The 'use' of a highly-skewed equilibrium towards E*:D for a promising drug is logical for the following reasons: (i) it increases the affinity for the drug by this coupled equilibrium, (ii) it prolongs the residence time of the drug on the target due to the often slow reverse rate, (iii) it is specific for each drug as it happens after the drug binding, and (iv) it can add selectivity for the targets because it likely involves residues more remote from the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical consequence of the induced-fit mechanism.

claim: A highly-skewed equilibrium towards E*:D prolongs the residence time of the drug on the target due to the often slow reverse rate.
source: The 'use' of a highly-skewed equilibrium towards E*:D for a promising drug is logical for the following reasons: (i) it increases the affinity for the drug by this coupled equilibrium, (ii) it prolongs the residence time of the drug on the target due to the often slow reverse rate, (iii) it is specific for each drug as it happens after the drug binding, and (iv) it can add selectivity for the targets because it likely involves residues more remote from the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical consequence of the induced-fit mechanism.

claim: The induced-fit step is specific for each drug as it happens after the drug binding.
source: The 'use' of a highly-skewed equilibrium towards E*:D for a promising drug is logical for the following reasons: (i) it increases the affinity for the drug by this coupled equilibrium, (ii) it prolongs the residence time of the drug on the target due to the often slow reverse rate, (iii) it is specific for each drug as it happens after the drug binding, and (iv) it can add selectivity for the targets because it likely involves residues more remote from the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical consequence of the induced-fit mechanism.

claim: The induced-fit step can add selectivity for the targets because it likely involves residues more remote from the active site.
source: The 'use' of a highly-skewed equilibrium towards E*:D for a promising drug is logical for the following reasons: (i) it increases the affinity for the drug by this coupled equilibrium, (ii) it prolongs the residence time of the drug on the target due to the often slow reverse rate, (iii) it is specific for each drug as it happens after the drug binding, and (iv) it can add selectivity for the targets because it likely involves residues more remote from the active site.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion as a logical consequence of the induced-fit mechanism.

claim: An increased drug residence time has significant pharmacological advantages as it can lead to a prolonged biological effect, a decrease of side effects, and a lower risk of metabolic drug modification.
source: An increased drug residence time has significant pharmacological advantages as it can lead to a prolonged biological effect, a decrease of side effects, and a lower risk of metabolic drug modification.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on pharmacological knowledge.

claim: Conformational selection by definition weakens the overall ligand affinity.
source: Based on our results, we argue that conformational selection of the DFG-state by ATP-competitive inhibitors is a mistakenly pursued concept in drug design for the following reasons: (i) conformational selection by definition weakens the overall ligand affinity, (ii) active site binders are automatically inhibitors, therefore selective binding to a specific DFG-state has no advantage (Badrinarayan and Sastry, 2014; Liu and Gray, 2006), (iii) kinases interconvert between both states.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the kinetic data and thermodynamic principles.

claim: Active site binders are automatically inhibitors, therefore selective binding to a specific DFG-state has no advantage.
source: Based on our results, we argue that conformational selection of the DFG-state by ATP-competitive inhibitors is a mistakenly pursued concept in drug design for the following reasons: (i) conformational selection by definition weakens the overall ligand affinity, (ii) active site binders are automatically inhibitors, therefore selective binding to a specific DFG-state has no advantage (Badrinarayan and Sastry, 2014; Liu and Gray, 2006), (iii) kinases interconvert between both states.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion with supporting citations.

claim: Kinases interconvert between both DFG states.
source: Based on our results, we argue that conformational selection of the DFG-state by ATP-competitive inhibitors is a mistakenly pursued concept in drug design for the following reasons: (i) conformational selection by definition weakens the overall ligand affinity, (ii) active site binders are automatically inhibitors, therefore selective binding to a specific DFG-state has no advantage (Badrinarayan and Sastry, 2014; Liu and Gray, 2006), (iii) kinases interconvert between both states.
evidence: This is stated in the discussion based on the kinetic and structural data.

claim: Future design efforts should focus on understanding and exploiting induced-fit steps.
source: Our data suggest that future design efforts should be focusing on understanding and exploiting induced-fit steps.
